items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next. Related links: Research Focus newsletter on LinkedIn (opens in new tab) ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents Code Understanding is a Bottleneck for Coding Agents TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills from Offline Telemetry Why Copilot use looks so similar across industries, and what that misses (opens in new tab) Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools New AI framework bridges a critical gap in mid-range weather forecasts BioEmu2 in public preview (opens in new tab) Chapters 00:48: A self-improving agentic framework (opens in new tab) 01:35: Understanding coding agent success and failure (opens in new tab) 02:29: Evolving agent skills with activity logs (opens in new tab) 03:22: Looking beyond similarities in AI use (opens in new tab) 04:15: Helping teachers make more time for teaching (opens in new tab) 04:52: Improving extended-range weather forecasting (opens in new tab) 05:42: BioEmu2 now available in public preview (opens in new tab) 06:32: Final thoughts (opens in new tab) Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast : Apple Podcasts Email Android Spotify RSS Feed Transcript [MUSIC] SOWBHAGYA SURESH: Hi, I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Welcome to Microsoft Research Focus . You’ve probably read our newsletter. And now you can get highlights from across the research community at Microsoft here, on YouTube, and major podcast platforms. Whether you read, watch, or listen to it, Research Focus is your source for research news at Microsoft. Coming up in this edition: what everyday AI use reveals about the way we work; how a new AI model could help scientists better understand proteins; a new approach to improving weather forecasts weeks in advance; and more. So here’s what’s new. A self-improving agentic framework More and more, AI agents are handling tasks that are complex. [MUSIC FADES] Tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, and interactions with external tools. But how can we count on AI agents to do the work if their ability to adjust when things go wrong may require a lot of resources with no guarantees of a better result? A new self-improving framework called ForkPilot learns when it’s worth revisiting earlier decisions to find a different approach and adapts its strategy based on new outcomes. Tested across six benchmarks and leading AI models, ForkPilot measures up to the best existing methods while reducing AI processing demands by up to 59%. These results suggest that AI agents can solve complex problems more reliably and efficiently, making them more practical and cost-effective to deploy at scale. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Understanding coding agent success and failure Coding agents execute user queries by reasoning about, editing, and running code. Understanding why these agents fail is critical if we want to build more capable and reliable coding agents. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks often make it difficult to identify which factors contribute to success or failure. CABRA is a framework for generating coding challenges from scratch. It lets researchers increase complexity in a controlled way and pinpoints the skills that are most difficult for agents. Across thousands of generated challenges, the researchers found that agents often overcame coding problems by using tools. Yet the agents still struggled when they needed to understand unfamiliar codebases. The findings suggest that understanding existing code, rather than modifying it, remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing more effective coding agents. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Evolving agent skills with activity logs Computer-use agents are AI systems that are designed to complete tasks that require clicking and typing. They can fill in forms, process requests, and navigate websites. To do this effectively, they need to learn the procedures that people use to get work done. User activity logs can offer a way to capture this knowledge. But activity logs typically don’t record the intent behind each action and often combine tasks. The new framework TeleTune learns reusable skills and workflows from these logs. It also infers the task goals associated with the sequences of actions. In evaluations across software and browser tasks, TeleTune outperformed existing approaches. By learning from existing activity, TeleTune offers a scalable way to help AI agents adapt to unfamiliar software and carry out complex, multi-step workflows [TRANSITION MUSIC] Looking beyond similarities in AI use (opens in new tab) Workers across industries may appear to be using AI in surprisingly similar ways, but a closer look reveals a different story. Microsoft researchers analyzed aggregated Copilot Chat activity across a broad range of customer categories and found that editing documents led all classified activities, accounting for more than 20 percent. But when researchers set aside the 20 most common activities, differences between customer categories became substantially more pronounced. The most common uses of AI may be hiding important differences in how organizations use it for more specialized work. For business leaders, the takeaway is clear: don’t assume you have the same AI needs as others in your industry. Finding the right opportunities means looking beyond usage statistics to understand what employees actually do, how they work, and what outcomes matter most. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Helping teachers make more time for teaching A new study shows how Shiksha Copilot—a human-in-the-loop AI tool—could transform teacher workflows in Global South classrooms. The study in low-resource schools in India found the tool reduced the time teachers spent on bilingual lesson planning and bureaucracy. That gave them more time to craft more engaging classroom activities. More than a thousand teachers participated, and many reported reduced stress levels and a positive impression of how AI can help them. These teachers actively engaged with Shiksha Copilot, using their professional expertise to adapt and repurpose materials to suit their own classrooms. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Improving extended-range weather forecasting Ten-day weather forecasts have become remarkably dependable. But what about the weeks that follow? The two-to-six-week window remains a major challenge for forecasting models, which is a problem. That’s when a wide range of critical decisions get made related to farming, managing wildfires, and preparing for extreme weather. A new machine-learning framework called Probabilistic Bias Correction, or PBC , is helping close that gap. PBC learns from a weather model’s past mistakes and helps correct them. And the early results are promising. PBC took top honors in a global competition focused on improving extended-range forecasting. It’s also being deployed in Kenya, where it’s helping improve critical monsoon forecasts for farmers. This development could help make weather predictions more useful across a broad range of applications. [TRANSITION MUSIC] BioEmu2 now available in public preview (opens in new tab) BioEmu2, a new foundation model for understanding biomolecular structure, dynamics, and function, is now available in public preview. Developed by the Microsoft Research AI for Science team, BioEmu2 builds on Biomolecular Emulator, a deep-learning model designed to help scientists better understand how proteins work. That understanding could have important implications for medicine. By learning more about how proteins function, scientists could move closer to developing more effective medications that enhance beneficial protein activity or prevent proteins from causing harm. Go to the BioEmu2 Microsoft Research GitHub repository (opens in new tab) to explore the model and learn more. [MUSIC] And that’s your Research Focus . From more capable AI agents to better weather forecasting, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring at Microsoft. Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by following Microsoft Research on major social platforms. I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Thanks so much for tuning in. We’ll see you in the next Microsoft Research Focus. [MUSIC FADES] Show more Opens in a new tab Meet the authors Sowbhagya Suresh Program Manager Learn more Research Areas Artificial intelligence

items.content: Simulation / Modeling / Design Unlocking Tensor Core Performance for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials Oct 29, 2026 By Anoushka Bhutani , Atul Thakur , Erica Tsai , Kristopher Keipert and Michele Ceriotti Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary BF16x9 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs accelerates large GEMMs in the Point Edge Transformer by 2.2–2.5x for a 17,280-atom system and 1.2–1.4x for a 192-atom system, with error below the model’s own non-determinism. TF32x3 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs speeds up major GEMMs by 1.7–1.9x and the full molecular dynamics step by up to 1.5x while keeping force error near the FP32 baseline. TF32x3 preserves potential-energy smoothness and energy conservation in NVE trajectories, matching FP32 behavior where one-pass TF32 shows drift and roughness. In structural relaxation of a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab, TF32x3 converges in 218–222 steps with a 1.5x per-step speedup, while one-pass TF32 fails to reach the force tolerance even after 1,000 steps. Next Steps Read the cuBLAS documentation to enable BF16x9 on Blackwell GPUs. Review the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit documentation for TF32x3 integration examples. Explore the UPET repository for PET model checkpoints and usage details. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Atomistic simulations help researchers understand how molecules and materials behave, from chemical reactions and phase transitions to mechanical failure. These simulations come with a cost-accuracy trade-off. Quantum-mechanical methods such as density functional theory (DFT) can provide accurate energies and forces, but their computational cost often limits their use for large systems or long simulations. Classical interatomic potentials are much faster, but their fixed functional forms limit accuracy and generalizability across different atomic environments. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) help bridge this gap. They use neural networks to predict potential energies and interatomic forces at a fraction of the cost, enabling researchers to study larger systems and longer timescales while retaining much of the required accuracy. Running an MLIP efficiently, however, presents its own challenge. Atomistic simulations are sensitive to small errors that can accumulate over time and are most visible when computing forces, which are obtained by differentiating the predicted energy. During molecular dynamics simulations, these forces guide updates to atomic velocities and positions over many timesteps, making numerical precision important not only for physical accuracy but also for the stability of the resulting trajectory. For this reason, many MLIPs continue to run inference in FP32, even though modern NVIDIA GPUs offer substantially higher matrix-multiplication throughput through low-precision Tensor Core operations. Tensor Core methods for FP32 matrix multiplication offer a way to narrow that gap. They decompose each FP32 operand into lower-precision components, evaluate their cross-products on Tensor Cores, and recombine the results in FP32. This approach can increase matrix-multiplication throughput while retaining accuracy close to native FP32, without retraining or changing the model’s weights or architecture. In this post, we evaluate how Tensor Core FP32 methods perform in practice on the Point Edge Transformer (PET), a transformer-based MLIP developed by Lab COSMO at EPFL. PET spends much of its runtime in highly optimized general matrix multiplications (GEMMs), leaving limited headroom for further optimization and making it a demanding test case of whether these methods can deliver additional performance gains. We evaluate BF16x9 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and TF32x3 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, comparing kernel and end-to-end molecular dynamics performance and trajectory-level behavior. We further test the TF32x3 method for potential-energy smoothness, energy conservation, and structural relaxation. We show how these methods can accelerate MLIP inference while retaining behavior close to the FP32 baseline and outline how to evaluate them on other precision-sensitive scientific machine learning workloads. How Tensor Core FP32 closes the hardware gap Modern NVIDIA GPUs deliver substantially higher Tensor Core throughput for BF16 and TF32 than for FP32 matrix multiplication, creating a gap between the available throughput at lower precision and the precision requirements of many scientific workloads. Tensor Core FP32 methods help narrow this gap by decomposing FP32 operands into lower-precision components, evaluating selected products on Tensor Cores, and recombining them with FP32 accumulation. Depending on the method and workload, this can deliver accuracy at or near native FP32 while taking advantage of higher Tensor Core throughput. Figure 1. The BF16x9 algorithm on Blackwell GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into three scaled BF16 components, producing nine pairwise products that are accumulated in FP32 along five anti-diagonal bands On Blackwell GPUs, NVIDIA cuBLAS provides a BF16x9 Tensor Core path (Figure 1). Each FP32 operand is decomposed into three BF16 components, and nine pairwise products are recombined with the required scaling. cuBLAS can enable this path through the CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 environment variable, so compatible PyTorch GEMMs can use it without changing the model architecture or implementing a custom GEMM. Because this approach changes how GEMMs are evaluated, it may provide additional gains when combined with optimized graph construction, fused operations, custom kernels, and NVIDIA CUDA graphs. We did not measure the combined gain in this evaluation; it should be established end to end for each workload. Figure 2. The TF32x3 algorithm on Ampere GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into a leading TF32 component and a smaller residual component. The leading-by-leading and two leading-by-residual products are accumulated in FP32; the residual-by-residual product is omitted The TF32x3 method applies the same principle on Ampere GPUs (Figure 2). TF32x3 represents each FP32 operand using a leading TF32 component and a residual TF32 component. Unlike BF16x9, our TF32x3 implementation does not use scaling factors. It evaluates three cross-products and omits the residual-by-residual term, as shown in the following equation a ⋅ b ≈ a hi b hi + a hi b lo + a lo b hi a \cdot b \approx a_{\mathrm{hi}}b_{\mathrm{hi}} + a_{\mathrm{hi}}b_{\mathrm{lo}} + a_{\mathrm{lo}}b_{\mathrm{hi}} NVIDIA CUTLASS provides this approach through the OpMultiplyAddFastF32 operator. Inputs and outputs remain in FP32. Tensor Cores execute the three TF32 products with accumulation in FP32. Benchmarking Tensor Core FP32 matrix math on PET We evaluated the 26M-parameter PET-MAD small checkpoint ( pet-mad-s-v1.6.0-nn-32 ) on a 192-atom water box and a 17,280-atom supercell. We also evaluated the 255M-parameter large checkpoint ( pet-mad-m-v1.6.0 ) on the 192-atom system. We compared predicted energies, forces, and stresses with those from the native FP32 path. BF16x9 method on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with compute capability 10.0 or 10.3, cuBLAS supports enabling BF16x9 through an environment variable, math mode, or compute type (requested with CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_EMULATED_16BFX9 , CUBLAS_FP32_EMULATED_BF16X9_MATH , or CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 ). No model-code changes are required to use this path for single-precision general matrix multiplication (SGEMM). Figure 3. With BF16x9 Tensor Core math for SGEMMs, large GEMMs in the PET model were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload and 1.2–1.4x for the 192-atom workload Figure 4. MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager BF16x9 modes, relative to compiled FP32, on a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell With BF16x9 on Blackwell, large GEMMs in PET were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload (Figure 3). Figure 4 compares MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager strategies against compiled FP32. 192-atom system: The performant strategy sped up the MD step by 1.2x, while the eager strategy achieved 1.1x. 17,280-atom system: The performant strategy achieved a 1.7x speedup, while the eager strategy achieved 1.4x. The performant strategy uses BF16x9 when cuBLAS expects it to be faster; the eager strategy uses it whenever the operation supports it. Importantly, the error due to the BF16x9 Tensor Core method is below the model’s own level of non-determinism. This result is significant because PET already expresses much of its runtime as optimized GEMM work, and yet the BF16x9 path exposed performance headroom without retraining the model, changing its transformer architecture, or writing custom kernels. TF32x3 method on Ampere GPUs On Ampere GPUs, we implemented TF32x3 by replacing PET’s standard nn.Linear layers with a custom TF32Linear layer that calls a CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel. CUTLASS C++ provides a reference implementation of this approach in Example 27 . The key setting in the PET implementation is: C++ cutlass::arch::OpMultiplyAddFastF32 This selects CUTLASS’s fast, accurate FP32 multiplication mode. The kernel represents each FP32 operand as leading and residual TF32 components. Tensor Cores then evaluate three products—leading-by-leading and the two leading-by-residual products—and accumulate them in FP32. The smallest residual-by-residual product is omitted. The CUTLASS C++ operator is declared with float inputs and outputs. PET therefore continues to supply ordinary FP32 activations and weights and receives an FP32 result; from the rest of the model’s perspective, the layer behaves like a standard nn.Linear . Only the implementation of the underlying matrix multiplication changes. The C++ example is written for sm80 (Ampere) and can also be compiled for sm90 (Hopper). The custom TF32Linear module replaces compatible PyTorch linear layers and performs their matrix multiplications using the CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel while preserving the trained weights, bias, and input shape. Because PET calculates forces by differentiating predicted energies, TF32x3 is also used to propagate gradients to the layer inputs. This ensures that both energy and force calculations use TF32x3 Tensor Core arithmetic. Weight gradients use the standard PyTorch path, but they are not required during fixed-weight inference. Figure 5. TF32x3 Tensor Core math accelerates large PET SGEMMs on an NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU by 1.7–1.9x relative to native FP32 for the 17,280-atom workload Figure 6. MD-step speedup and single-point accuracy for one-pass TF32 and TF32x3, each measured against its own FP32 baseline Across PET’s major linear-layer shapes on A100, TF32x3 accelerated GEMMs by approximately 1.7–1.9x (Figure 5). Figure 6 compares MD-step speedup and single-point accuracy for one-pass TF32 and TF32x3, each measured against its corresponding FP32 baseline. One-pass TF32 achieved higher speedups, but at a greater cost to accuracy and trajectory stability (Figures 6–7). Small checkpoint (26M parameters): Results are shown for a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell. TF32x3 kept the force error to roughly three times the difference between FP32 runs after recompilation and sped up the MD step by 1.5x on the larger system. Large checkpoint (255M parameters): On the 192-atom system, TF32x3 achieved a 1.4x speedup, compared with 1.2x for the small checkpoint. Its force error was 3.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV/Å, essentially unchanged from the small checkpoint. Validating physical consistency For molecular simulation, matching isolated energy and force predictions is only the first test of numerical fidelity. Forces are gradients of the learned potential-energy surface and are integrated over many timesteps, so even small numerical irregularities can roughen the surface, destabilize trajectories, or produce unphysical energy drift. The promise of the Tensor Core FP32 method is therefore especially compelling: it can unlock Tensor Core performance for matrix multiplications while preserving the smooth and stable behavior expected from FP32. We tested potential-energy smoothness and energy conservation using two separate tests (Figure 7). To test energy smoothness, we dragged a single CO molecule rigidly away from an on-top site of a Pt(111) slab and evaluated the total energy at 60 carbon heights from 1.2 to 6.0 Å in steps of 8.1 × 10⁻² Å. TF32x3 followed the smooth FP32 CO/Pt(111) energy curve, while one-pass TF32 introduced visible point-to-point variations. In a separate NVE simulation of a 192-atom water box, FP32 and TF32x3 showed comparable bounded energy fluctuations, while one-pass TF32 showed a larger systematic drift. These results show that TF32x3 preserved potential-energy smoothness and maintained energy conservation in the tested systems, not just single-point accuracy. Figure 7. CO/Pt(111) potential-energy curve and total-energy drift during a 30 ps NVE trajectory of a 192-atom water box Testing structural relaxation Structural relaxation also tests numerical fidelity as the optimizer repeatedly uses predicted forces to update the atomic geometry. Small force inconsistencies can alter the optimization path, increase the number of steps required, or prevent the system from reaching the desired force tolerance. We relaxed a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab using PET and the FIRE2 optimizer with the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit. Across three replicates, FP32 converged in 218 steps and TF32x3 in 218–222 steps; every run reached the 1.0 × 10⁻³ eV/Å force tolerance. With one-pass TF32, all three replicates failed to converge within the 500-step limit, and forces plateaued around 1.2 × 10⁻³ eV/Å. TF32x3 accelerated each optimization step by 1.5x while matching the FP32 convergence rate and criterion (Figure 8). One-pass TF32 achieved a 2.0x per-step speedup but failed to converge even after doubling the optimization step limit to 1,000 steps. These results highlight the practical value of the Tensor Core path: substantial acceleration without sacrificing the convergence behavior of the FP32 workflow. Figure 8. Per-step speedup and force convergence for FP32, TF32x3, and one-pass TF32 across three replicates of a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab (Co₁₀₈Cr₁₀₈Fe₁₀₈Mn₁₀₇Ni₁₀₈) relaxed using PET and the FIRE2 optimizer in NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit Limitations and decision criteria End-to-end gains depend on system size and the share of runtime spent in GEMMs. Small systems generally benefit less because launch overhead, neighbor processing, graph operations, and other non-GEMM work make up a larger portion of the runtime. Larger systems benefit more when GEMMs account for more of the work. TF32x3’s performance also depends on kernel tuning for the model’s matrix shapes and hardware. Numerical behavior depends on the Tensor Core strategy used. In matrix-multiplication tests, BF16x9 matched or exceeded native FP32 accuracy against an FP64 reference, supporting its use as a drop-in replacement for FP32 GEMMs on supported hardware. TF32x3 has a slightly different accuracy profile and should be validated against the model’s accuracy and physical-stability requirements. Conclusion Tensor Core FP32 methods improved PET performance without retraining or changing the model architecture. TF32x3 accelerated major GEMMs on A100 by up to 1.9x and the complete molecular dynamics step by up to 1.5x. BF16x9 accelerated major GEMMs on an NVIDIA B300 Tensor Core GPU by up to 2.5x and the complete step by up to 1.7x. As demonstrated for TF32x3, Tensor Core methods preserve behavior close to FP32 in the tested energy-conservation and structural-relaxation workflows. These results support evaluating the methods in other MLIPs and precision-sensitive scientific machine learning models whose runtime is dominated by large FP32 GEMMs. Neither of the Tensor Core FP32 strategies requires retraining or an architectural redesign. Each can therefore be evaluated as an independent performance layer and combined with other software optimizations when the workload supports it. Try TF32x3 or BF16x9 Tensor Core methods with your model today—no retraining or architectural changes needed. Learn more in the cuBLAS documentation and the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit documentation . Explore the PET models in the UPET repository . Acknowledgments We’d like to thank Nikita Fedik, Harun Bayraktar, Gregory Thomsen, and Vamsi Sripathi for their contributions to this post. items.raw_text: Simulation / Modeling / Design Unlocking Tensor Core Performance for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials Oct 29, 2026 By Anoushka Bhutani , Atul Thakur , Erica Tsai , Kristopher Keipert and Michele Ceriotti Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary BF16x9 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs accelerates large GEMMs in the Point Edge Transformer by 2.2–2.5x for a 17,280-atom system and 1.2–1.4x for a 192-atom system, with error below the model’s own non-determinism. TF32x3 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs speeds up major GEMMs by 1.7–1.9x and the full molecular dynamics step by up to 1.5x while keeping force error near the FP32 baseline. TF32x3 preserves potential-energy smoothness and energy conservation in NVE trajectories, matching FP32 behavior where one-pass TF32 shows drift and roughness. In structural relaxation of a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab, TF32x3 converges in 218–222 steps with a 1.5x per-step speedup, while one-pass TF32 fails to reach the force tolerance even after 1,000 steps. Next Steps Read the cuBLAS documentation to enable BF16x9 on Blackwell GPUs. Review the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit documentation for TF32x3 integration examples. Explore the UPET repository for PET model checkpoints and usage details. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Atomistic simulations help researchers understand how molecules and materials behave, from chemical reactions and phase transitions to mechanical failure. These simulations come with a cost-accuracy trade-off. Quantum-mechanical methods such as density functional theory (DFT) can provide accurate energies and forces, but their computational cost often limits their use for large systems or long simulations. Classical interatomic potentials are much faster, but their fixed functional forms limit accuracy and generalizability across different atomic environments. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) help bridge this gap. They use neural networks to predict potential energies and interatomic forces at a fraction of the cost, enabling researchers to study larger systems and longer timescales while retaining much of the required accuracy. Running an MLIP efficiently, however, presents its own challenge. Atomistic simulations are sensitive to small errors that can accumulate over time and are most visible when computing forces, which are obtained by differentiating the predicted energy. During molecular dynamics simulations, these forces guide updates to atomic velocities and positions over many timesteps, making numerical precision important not only for physical accuracy but also for the stability of the resulting trajectory. For this reason, many MLIPs continue to run inference in FP32, even though modern NVIDIA GPUs offer substantially higher matrix-multiplication throughput through low-precision Tensor Core operations. Tensor Core methods for FP32 matrix multiplication offer a way to narrow that gap. They decompose each FP32 operand into lower-precision components, evaluate their cross-products on Tensor Cores, and recombine the results in FP32. This approach can increase matrix-multiplication throughput while retaining accuracy close to native FP32, without retraining or changing the model’s weights or architecture. In this post, we evaluate how Tensor Core FP32 methods perform in practice on the Point Edge Transformer (PET), a transformer-based MLIP developed by Lab COSMO at EPFL. PET spends much of its runtime in highly optimized general matrix multiplications (GEMMs), leaving limited headroom for further optimization and making it a demanding test case of whether these methods can deliver additional performance gains. We evaluate BF16x9 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and TF32x3 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, comparing kernel and end-to-end molecular dynamics performance and trajectory-level behavior. We further test the TF32x3 method for potential-energy smoothness, energy conservation, and structural relaxation. We show how these methods can accelerate MLIP inference while retaining behavior close to the FP32 baseline and outline how to evaluate them on other precision-sensitive scientific machine learning workloads. How Tensor Core FP32 closes the hardware gap Modern NVIDIA GPUs deliver substantially higher Tensor Core throughput for BF16 and TF32 than for FP32 matrix multiplication, creating a gap between the available throughput at lower precision and the precision requirements of many scientific workloads. Tensor Core FP32 methods help narrow this gap by decomposing FP32 operands into lower-precision components, evaluating selected products on Tensor Cores, and recombining them with FP32 accumulation. Depending on the method and workload, this can deliver accuracy at or near native FP32 while taking advantage of higher Tensor Core throughput. Figure 1. The BF16x9 algorithm on Blackwell GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into three scaled BF16 components, producing nine pairwise products that are accumulated in FP32 along five anti-diagonal bands On Blackwell GPUs, NVIDIA cuBLAS provides a BF16x9 Tensor Core path (Figure 1). Each FP32 operand is decomposed into three BF16 components, and nine pairwise products are recombined with the required scaling. cuBLAS can enable this path through the CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 environment variable, so compatible PyTorch GEMMs can use it without changing the model architecture or implementing a custom GEMM. Because this approach changes how GEMMs are evaluated, it may provide additional gains when combined with optimized graph construction, fused operations, custom kernels, and NVIDIA CUDA graphs. We did not measure the combined gain in this evaluation; it should be established end to end for each workload. Figure 2. The TF32x3 algorithm on Ampere GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into a leading TF32 component and a smaller residual component. The leading-by-leading and two leading-by-residual products are accumulated in FP32; the residual-by-residual product is omitted The TF32x3 method applies the same principle on Ampere GPUs (Figure 2). TF32x3 represents each FP32 operand using a leading TF32 component and a residual TF32 component. Unlike BF16x9, our TF32x3 implementation does not use scaling factors. It evaluates three cross-products and omits the residual-by-residual term, as shown in the following equation a ⋅ b ≈ a hi b hi + a hi b lo + a lo b hi a \cdot b \approx a_{\mathrm{hi}}b_{\mathrm{hi}} + a_{\mathrm{hi}}b_{\mathrm{lo}} + a_{\mathrm{lo}}b_{\mathrm{hi}} NVIDIA CUTLASS provides this approach through the OpMultiplyAddFastF32 operator. Inputs and outputs remain in FP32. Tensor Cores execute the three TF32 products with accumulation in FP32. Benchmarking Tensor Core FP32 matrix math on PET We evaluated the 26M-parameter PET-MAD small checkpoint ( pet-mad-s-v1.6.0-nn-32 ) on a 192-atom water box and a 17,280-atom supercell. We also evaluated the 255M-parameter large checkpoint ( pet-mad-m-v1.6.0 ) on the 192-atom system. We compared predicted energies, forces, and stresses with those from the native FP32 path. BF16x9 method on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with compute capability 10.0 or 10.3, cuBLAS supports enabling BF16x9 through an environment variable, math mode, or compute type (requested with CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_EMULATED_16BFX9 , CUBLAS_FP32_EMULATED_BF16X9_MATH , or CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 ). No model-code changes are required to use this path for single-precision general matrix multiplication (SGEMM). Figure 3. With BF16x9 Tensor Core math for SGEMMs, large GEMMs in the PET model were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload and 1.2–1.4x for the 192-atom workload Figure 4. MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager BF16x9 modes, relative to compiled FP32, on a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell With BF16x9 on Blackwell, large GEMMs in PET were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload (Figure 3). Figure 4 compares MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager strategies against compiled FP32. 192-atom system: The performant strategy sped up the MD step by 1.2x, while the eager strategy achieved 1.1x. 17,280-atom system: The performant strategy achieved a 1.7x speedup, while the eager strategy achieved 1.4x. The performant strategy uses BF16x9 when cuBLAS expects it to be faster; the eager strategy uses it whenever the operation supports it. Importantly, the error due to the BF16x9 Tensor Core method is below the model’s own level of non-determinism. This result is significant because PET already expresses much of its runtime as optimized GEMM work, and yet the BF16x9 path exposed performance headroom without retraining the model, changing its transformer architecture, or writing custom kernels. TF32x3 method on Ampere GPUs On Ampere GPUs, we implemented TF32x3 by replacing PET’s standard nn.Linear layers with a custom TF32Linear layer that calls a CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel. CUTLASS C++ provides a reference implementation of this approach in Example 27 . The key setting in the PET implementation is: C++ cutlass::arch::OpMultiplyAddFastF32 This selects CUTLASS’s fast, accurate FP32 multiplication mode. The kernel represents each FP32 operand as leading and residual TF32 components. Tensor Cores then evaluate three products—leading-by-leading and the two leading-by-residual products—and accumulate them in FP32. The smallest residual-by-residual product is omitted. The CUTLASS C++ operator is declared with float inputs and outputs. PET therefore continues to supply ordinary FP32 activations and weights and receives an FP32 result; from the rest of the model’s perspective, the layer behaves like a standard nn.Linear . Only the implementation of the underlying matrix multiplication changes. The C++ example is written for sm80 (Ampere) and can also be compiled for sm90 (Hopper). The custom TF32Linear module replaces compatible PyTorch linear layers and performs their matrix multiplications using the CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel while preserving the trained weights, bias, and input shape. Because PET calculates forces by differentiating predicted energies, TF32x3 is also used to propagate gradients to the layer inputs. This ensures that both energy and force calculations use TF32x3 Tensor Core arithmetic. Weight gradients use the standard PyTorch path, but they are not required during fixed-weight inference. Figure 5. TF32x3 Tensor Core math accelerates large PET SGEMMs on an NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU by 1.7–1.9x relative to native FP32 for the 17,280-atom workload Figure 6. MD-step speedup and single-point accuracy for one-pass TF32 and TF32x3, each measured against its own FP32 baseline Across PET’s major linear-layer shapes on A100, TF32x3 accelerated GEMMs by approximately 1.7–1.9x (Figure 5). Figure 6 compares MD-step speedup and single-point accuracy for one-pass TF32 and TF32x3, each measured against its corresponding FP32 baseline. One-pass TF32 achieved higher speedups, but at a greater cost to accuracy and trajectory stability (Figures 6–7). Small checkpoint (26M parameters): Results are shown for a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell. TF32x3 kept the force error to roughly three times the difference between FP32 runs after recompilation and sped up the MD step by 1.5x on the larger system. Large checkpoint (255M parameters): On the 192-atom system, TF32x3 achieved a 1.4x speedup, compared with 1.2x for the small checkpoint. Its force error was 3.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV/Å, essentially unchanged from the small checkpoint. Validating physical consistency For molecular simulation, matching isolated energy and force predictions is only the first test of numerical fidelity. Forces are gradients of the learned potential-energy surface and are integrated over many timesteps, so even small numerical irregularities can roughen the surface, destabilize trajectories, or produce unphysical energy drift. The promise of the Tensor Core FP32 method is therefore especially compelling: it can unlock Tensor Core performance for matrix multiplications while preserving the smooth and stable behavior expected from FP32. We tested potential-energy smoothness and energy conservation using two separate tests (Figure 7). To test energy smoothness, we dragged a single CO molecule rigidly away from an on-top site of a Pt(111) slab and evaluated the total energy at 60 carbon heights from 1.2 to 6.0 Å in steps of 8.1 × 10⁻² Å. TF32x3 followed the smooth FP32 CO/Pt(111) energy curve, while one-pass TF32 introduced visible point-to-point variations. In a separate NVE simulation of a 192-atom water box, FP32 and TF32x3 showed comparable bounded energy fluctuations, while one-pass TF32 showed a larger systematic drift. These results show that TF32x3 preserved potential-energy smoothness and maintained energy conservation in the tested systems, not just single-point accuracy. Figure 7. CO/Pt(111) potential-energy curve and total-energy drift during a 30 ps NVE trajectory of a 192-atom water box Testing structural relaxation Structural relaxation also tests numerical fidelity as the optimizer repeatedly uses predicted forces to update the atomic geometry. Small force inconsistencies can alter the optimization path, increase the number of steps required, or prevent the system from reaching the desired force tolerance. We relaxed a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab using PET and the FIRE2 optimizer with the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit. Across three replicates, FP32 converged in 218 steps and TF32x3 in 218–222 steps; every run reached the 1.0 × 10⁻³ eV/Å force tolerance. With one-pass TF32, all three replicates failed to converge within the 500-step limit, and forces plateaued around 1.2 × 10⁻³ eV/Å. TF32x3 accelerated each optimization step by 1.5x while matching the FP32 convergence rate and criterion (Figure 8). One-pass TF32 achieved a 2.0x per-step speedup but failed to converge even after doubling the optimization step limit to 1,000 steps. These results highlight the practical value of the Tensor Core path: substantial acceleration without sacrificing the convergence behavior of the FP32 workflow. Figure 8. Per-step speedup and force convergence for FP32, TF32x3, and one-pass TF32 across three replicates of a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab (Co₁₀₈Cr₁₀₈Fe₁₀₈Mn₁₀₇Ni₁₀₈) relaxed using PET and the FIRE2 optimizer in NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit Limitations and decision criteria End-to-end gains depend on system size and the share of runtime spent in GEMMs. Small systems generally benefit less because launch overhead, neighbor processing, graph operations, and other non-GEMM work make up a larger portion of the runtime. Larger systems benefit more when GEMMs account for more of the work. TF32x3’s performance also depends on kernel tuning for the model’s matrix shapes and hardware. Numerical behavior depends on the Tensor Core strategy used. In matrix-multiplication tests, BF16x9 matched or exceeded native FP32 accuracy against an FP64 reference, supporting its use as a drop-in replacement for FP32 GEMMs on supported hardware. TF32x3 has a slightly different accuracy profile and should be validated against the model’s accuracy and physical-stability requirements. Conclusion Tensor Core FP32 methods improved PET performance without retraining or changing the model architecture. TF32x3 accelerated major GEMMs on A100 by up to 1.9x and the complete molecular dynamics step by up to 1.5x. BF16x9 accelerated major GEMMs on an NVIDIA B300 Tensor Core GPU by up to 2.5x and the complete step by up to 1.7x. As demonstrated for TF32x3, Tensor Core methods preserve behavior close to FP32 in the tested energy-conservation and structural-relaxation workflows. These results support evaluating the methods in other MLIPs and precision-sensitive scientific machine learning models whose runtime is dominated by large FP32 GEMMs. Neither of the Tensor Core FP32 strategies requires retraining or an architectural redesign. Each can therefore be evaluated as an independent performance layer and combined with other software optimizations when the workload supports it. items.content: Back to Articles AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 6 Mattt mattt Follow Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses , for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers , and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions ) Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ) ] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface , and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses , for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers , and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions ) Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ) ] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface , and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. items.content: Back to Articles Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 25 +19 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ], ) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , ) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 , ) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" , ) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data. PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices. In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member. Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. References ECMWF: Ensemble weather forecasting NOAA: North American Multi-Model Ensemble FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting Tiny Time Mixers (TTMs): Fast Pre-trained Models for Enhanced Zero/Few-Shot Forecasting of Multivariate Time Series Revisiting the Generic Transformer: Deconstructing a Strong Baseline for Time Series Foundation Models Forecast combinations: an over 50-year review Smith and Wallis (2009), A Simple Explanation of the Forecast Combination Puzzle Models mentioned in this article 5 Spaces mentioned in this article 1 More from this author ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model 27 October 20, 2026 Your Agent Aced the Task. Look It Up Published October 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 31 +25 David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow In a previous post , we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. Look up a model The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler ( neuronx-cc ) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" ) df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.
